newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia warns PNG against mercenary plan.
newsitem.headline: Australia warns PNG against mercenary plan.

text.p: Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer warned the Papua New Guinea government on Monday not to go ahead with a plan to use mercenaries against secessionist rebels on Bougainville island.

Downer was reacting to Australian newspaper reports that the South Pacific nation planned to bring in up to 150 Africa-based mercenaries to mount an operation to capture or kill the leaders of the pro-independence Bougainville Revolutionary Army.
The newspapers said the Papua New Guinea government had approved a A$36 million (US$27 million) covert operation to end the nine-year rebellion on Bougainville.

Downer said he had warned Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Julius Chan during a ministerial visit to Port Moresby last week that such a plan would significantly damage the country's international standing.
"It's a matter of profound concern to the (Australian) federal government that this is happening," Downer told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio.

"What I made clear to Sir Julius Chan and to other ministers...was that if there was a resumption of any military activity on Bougainville, then it would be regarded by Australia as absolutely disastrous," Downer said.
"I will use any vehicle which is reasonable that I possibly can to try to stop this operation going ahead, but of course I don't wish to act outside the law myself."
The Papua New Guinea government has refused to confirm or deny the mercenary plan, but the Australian High Commission in Port Moresby has reportedly warned Australians not to stay on Bougainville.

The Australian newspaper reported military cargo aircraft leased to Sandlines International, a subsidiary of the British-registered company Executive Outcomes, had been flying in and out of Jackson Airport in Port Moresby last week.
Executive Outcomes is Africa's best known private army and has helped Angola and Sierra Leone fight rebel threats.

The Australian said the mercenaries would stage a "surgical strike" targetting hardline rebel leaders on Bougainville, while a second operation by mercenaries would try to free five Papua New Guinea soldiers held captive by rebels.

Hundreds of people have died in direct fighting or from disease through a lack of medical supplies during the rebellion on Bougainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of the Papua New Guinea capital Port Moresby.
